title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
summary: A self-contained specification of the basic protocol for Internet electronic mail transport, SMTP. It covers how mail is handed from sender to server and between servers. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 5321.

plainLanguage.summary:
SMTP is the set of rules two mail servers use to pass a message along. One asks the other to send a message, names who it is from and who it is for, then hands over the text.

Every step gets a numbered answer, so the sending side always knows whether to carry on, wait, or give up.

questions: what do smtp reply codes mean
how does smtp find the mail server for a domain
subtitle: The rulebook for moving email between servers: the commands, the replies, and who does what when a message cannot be delivered.

tldr.problem: Internet mail needs a reliable, efficient way to hand a message from a sender to a destination, possibly through several intermediate hosts, with clear rules about who is responsible for it.
tldr.mechanism: An SMTP client opens a channel to a server and sends MAIL, RCPT and DATA commands that name the sender, the recipients and the message. The server answers each command with a numbered reply, and the next hop is found with DNS MX records.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2821 consolidated RFC 821 and related documents, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 5321, which is the current SMTP specification.

today: RFC 2821 was a Proposed Standard and it consolidated RFC 821 and a long series of updates to it. It has itself been obsoleted by RFC 5321, which is the current SMTP specification, and was updated by RFC 5336.

sections.title: What SMTP Is For
sections.content:
The objective of the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol is to transfer mail reliably and efficiently. SMTP is independent of the particular transmission subsystem and requires only a reliable ordered data stream channel. This document discusses transport over TCP, but other transports are possible.

An important feature of SMTP is its capability to transport mail across networks, usually called SMTP mail relaying. A network consists of the mutually accessible hosts on the public Internet, the mutually accessible hosts on a firewall-isolated intranet, or hosts in some other local or wide area environment. Using SMTP, a process can transfer mail to another process on the same network, or to some other network through a relay or gateway process accessible to both.

In this way, a mail message may pass through a number of intermediate relay or gateway hosts on its path from sender to ultimate recipient. The Mail eXchanger mechanisms of the domain name system are used to identify the appropriate next-hop destination for a message being transported, and intermediate hosts are usually determined through the DNS MX record rather than by explicit source routing.

This specification consolidates the original SMTP definition of RFC 821 with its later updates and extensions, and it also includes some additional material from RFC 1123 that required amplification. Where it moves beyond consolidation and actually differs from earlier documents, it supersedes them technically as well as textually. Although SMTP was designed as a mail transport and delivery protocol, the document also contains information important to its use as a mail submission protocol, as recommended for POP and IMAP.
sections.plainLanguage:
Mail rarely goes straight from the sender to the recipient. It usually passes through one or more servers, and each hop has to work out where to send it next.

This document is the consolidated rulebook for all of that, gathering the original standard and everything added to it since.

sections.title: The Basic Structure
sections.content:
When an SMTP client has a message to transmit, it establishes a two-way transmission channel to an SMTP server. The client's job is to transfer mail messages to one or more SMTP servers, or to report its failure to do so.

How a message is presented to the client, and how the client works out which domain names to transfer messages to, is a local matter not addressed by this document. In some cases the domain names will identify the final destinations of the message. In other cases, common with clients associated with POP or IMAP or with clients inside an isolated transport environment, the domain name identifies an intermediate destination through which all messages are to be relayed. Clients that transfer all traffic regardless of the target domain names, or that do not maintain queues for retrying messages that initially cannot be completed, may otherwise conform but are not considered fully capable. Fully capable implementations, including the relays used by these less capable ones, are expected to support all of the queuing, retrying and alternate address functions described in the specification.

An SMTP server may be the ultimate destination, an intermediate relay that takes on the role of a client after receiving the message, or a gateway that transports the message further using some protocol other than SMTP. The client generates commands and the server sends replies in response.

Message transfer can occur in a single connection between the original sender and the final recipient, or in a series of hops through intermediary systems. In either case a formal handoff of responsibility occurs: the protocol requires that a server accept responsibility for either delivering a message or properly reporting the failure to do so.

Once the channel is established and the initial handshake is complete, the client normally initiates a mail transaction, a series of commands specifying the originator and destination of the mail and transmitting the message content itself. When the same message is sent to multiple recipients, the protocol encourages transmitting only one copy of the data for all recipients at the same host.

The server responds to each command with a reply, which may say that the command was accepted, that more commands are expected, or that a temporary or permanent error exists. Commands naming the sender or recipients may include server-permitted service extension requests. The dialog is purposely lock-step, one command at a time, although this can be modified by mutually agreed extension requests such as command pipelining.

Once a message has been transmitted, the client may ask for the connection to be shut down or start another transaction. An SMTP client may also use a connection for ancillary services such as verification of email addresses or retrieval of mailing list subscriber addresses.
sections.plainLanguage:
One side asks, the other side answers. The asking side is the client, the answering side the server, and the server may be the final destination or simply pass the message on.

Whichever server accepts a message becomes responsible for it, either delivering it or saying clearly that it could not.

sections.title: The Commands and the Replies
sections.content:
The SMTP commands are character strings terminated by a carriage return and line feed. The commands themselves are alphabetic characters terminated by a space if parameters follow and by the line ending otherwise. In the interest of interoperability, receivers are encouraged to tolerate trailing white space before the terminating line ending.

A mail transaction involves several data objects passed as arguments to different commands. The reverse-path is the argument of MAIL, the forward-path is the argument of RCPT, and the mail data is the argument of DATA. These must be held pending the confirmation communicated by the end of mail data indication. The model is that distinct buffers hold the types of data objects: a reverse-path buffer, a forward-path buffer and a mail data buffer. Specific commands append information to a buffer or clear one or more buffers.

Several commands, RSET, DATA and QUIT, are specified as not permitting parameters. Absent specific extensions offered by the server and accepted by the client, clients must not send such parameters and servers should reject commands containing them as having invalid syntax.

EHLO and HELO identify the client to the server. The argument holds the fully-qualified domain name of the client if one is available. A client should start a session with EHLO. If the server supports service extensions it gives a successful, failure or error response; if it does not support them at all, in violation of the specification, it gives an error response. Older clients may use HELO instead, and servers must support HELO and reply to it properly. In any event a client must issue HELO or EHLO before starting a transaction. These commands, and a 250 reply to one of them, confirm that both sides are in the initial state, with no transaction in progress and all buffers cleared. The reply to EHLO is normally a multiline reply, each line holding a keyword and optionally parameters. Keywords may be written in any case but must always be recognised case-insensitively.

MAIL initiates a transaction in which the mail data is delivered to a server, which may deliver it to one or more mailboxes or pass it on. Its argument holds a reverse-path and may hold optional parameters, and it may generally be sent only when no transaction is in progress. The reverse-path consists of the sender mailbox; the historical option of a list of hosts before it is now deprecated, and in some kinds of reporting message, where a reply would cause a mail loop, the reverse-path may be null. MAIL clears the reverse-path, forward-path and mail data buffers and inserts the reverse-path information.

RCPT identifies an individual recipient, and several recipients are named by using the command several times. Its argument holds a forward-path and may hold optional parameters. Sending systems should not generate the optional list of hosts known as a source route, and receiving systems must recognise source route syntax but should strip it and use the domain name associated with the mailbox as if it had not been provided. Relay hosts should likewise strip or ignore source routes, and names must not be copied into the reverse-path. If the server receives an inappropriate request from a workstation trying to set the common network number, it must overwrite those values with preferred ones.

DATA transfers the message. The receiver normally sends a 354 response and then treats the following lines as mail data. The message ends with a line containing only a period, and the receiver then replies, normally with 250, to confirm acceptance.

RSET aborts the current transaction and resets the buffers. VRFY asks whether a mailbox exists, EXPN asks for the members of a mailing list, HELP asks for help, NOOP does nothing and expects a reply, and QUIT ends the session.

The replies use a three-digit code whose first digit carries the meaning. A 1yz reply is a positive preliminary answer, meaning the command was accepted but the action is held pending confirmation in that reply. A 2yz reply is a positive completion, meaning the action finished successfully and a new request may begin. A 3yz reply is a positive intermediate, meaning the command was accepted but the action is held pending further information, which is what DATA uses. A 4yz reply is a transient negative completion: the command was not accepted, the action did not occur, but the error is temporary and the action may be requested again. A 5yz reply is a permanent negative completion, meaning the action will not happen under any circumstances. A client that wants to know roughly what kind of error occurred can look at the second digit, and the third digit is reserved for the finest gradation of information.
sections.plainLanguage:
There are ten commands and each one gets a numbered answer.

The first digit of the number is what matters: two means it worked, three means send more, four means try again later, five means never going to work.

sections.title: Sizes and Timeouts
sections.content:
Several objects have required minimum and maximum sizes, and every implementation must be able to receive objects of at least these sizes. Objects larger than these should be avoided where possible, although some Internet mail constructs, such as encoded X.400 addresses, will often require larger objects; clients may attempt to transmit them but must be prepared for a server to reject them.

The maximum total length of a user name or other local-part is 64 characters. The maximum total length of a domain name or number is 255 characters. The maximum total length of a reverse-path or forward-path is 256 characters, including the punctuation and element separators. The maximum total length of a command line, including the command word and the line ending, is 512 characters, and SMTP extensions may be used to raise this. The maximum total length of a reply line, including the reply code and the line ending, is 512 characters, and more information may be conveyed through multiple-line replies. The maximum total length of a text line, including the line ending, is 1000 characters, not counting the leading dot duplicated for transparency, and this may also be increased by SMTP service extensions. The maximum total length of a message content, including headers and body, must be at least 64K octets, and since the introduction of Internet standards for multimedia mail, message lengths have grown dramatically, so message size restrictions should be avoided where possible.

An SMTP client must provide a timeout mechanism, and it must use per-command timeouts rather than timing the entire transaction. Timeouts should be easily reconfigurable, preferably without recompiling. A timer is set for each SMTP command and for each buffer of the data transfer, which means the overall timeout is inherently proportional to the size of the message.

Based on extensive experience with busy mail-relay hosts, the RFC recommends minimum per-command timeouts. The initial 220 message gets 5 minutes, so that a client can tell a failed TCP connection apart from a server that has accepted the connection but is delaying its greeting until its load permits more mail to be processed. The MAIL command gets 5 minutes and the RCPT command 5 minutes, the latter needing longer if mailing lists and aliases are processed rather than deferred. DATA initiation gets 2 minutes, which is the wait for the 354 reply. A data block gets 3 minutes, covering each send call transmitting a chunk of data. DATA termination gets 10 minutes while awaiting the 250 reply, because a spurious timeout at that point would be very wasteful and would typically result in multiple copies of the message, since it has already been sent and the server has accepted responsibility for it. An SMTP server should have a timeout of at least 5 minutes while awaiting the next command.
sections.plainLanguage:
The document sets a size limit for every part of an address and every kind of line, and a time limit for every step of a session.

The last timeout is the generous one. A server that is slow to confirm the end of a message is probably delivering it, and giving up would send it twice.

sections.title: Finding the Next Server
sections.content:
Once an SMTP client has identified a domain to which mail will be delivered for processing, a DNS lookup must be performed to resolve the domain name. The names are expected to be fully-qualified domain names; mechanisms for inferring them from partial names or local aliases are outside the specification and, because of a history of problems, are generally discouraged.

The lookup first tries to locate an MX record associated with the name. If a CNAME record is found instead, the resulting name is processed as if it were the initial name. If no MX records are found but an A record is found, that record is treated as if it were associated with an implicit MX record with a preference of 0, pointing to that host. If one or more MX records are found, SMTP systems must not use any A records associated with that name unless they are located using the MX records; the implicit MX rule applies only when there are no MX records present. If MX records are present but none of them are usable, this situation must be reported as an error.

When the lookup succeeds, the mapping can result in a list of alternative delivery addresses rather than a single address, because of multiple MX records, multihoming, or both. To provide reliable transmission, the client must be able to try and retry each of the relevant addresses in the list in order until a delivery attempt succeeds, though there may also be a configurable limit on how many alternates are tried. In any case the client should try at least two addresses.

Two kinds of information rank the host addresses. Multiple MX records carry a preference indication that must be used in sorting, with lower numbers more preferred. If there are multiple destinations with the same preference and no clear reason to favour one, the sender must randomize them to spread the load across the mail exchangers of that organisation. The destination host may also be multihomed, in which case the resolver returns a list of alternative IP addresses, ordered by decreasing preference if necessary, and SMTP must try them in the order presented. The capability to try multiple addresses is required, although specific installations may want to limit or disable it, and the question of whether a sender should retry using the different addresses of a multihomed host has been controversial. The main argument for using them is that it maximises the probability of timely delivery, and indeed sometimes the probability of any delivery; the counter-argument is that it may result in unnecessary resource use.

When an SMTP server receives a message with a destination for which it is a designated Mail eXchanger, it may relay the message, possibly after rewriting the MAIL FROM and RCPT TO addresses, make final delivery, or hand it off by some mechanism outside the SMTP transport environment. If it decides to relay without rewriting the address, it must sort the MX records to determine candidates, ordering them by preference with the lowest-numbered records most preferred. The relay host must then inspect the list for any of the names or addresses by which it might be known in mail transactions; if a matching record is found, all records at that preference level and the higher-numbered ones must be discarded. If no records remain, that is an error condition and the message must be returned as undeliverable. If records do remain, they should be tried, best preference first.

Two further obligations sit alongside. When the receiver accepts a piece of mail, by sending a 250 reply in response to DATA, it is accepting responsibility for delivering or relaying it, and must not lose the message for frivolous reasons such as a later crash or a predictable resource shortage. If a delivery fails after acceptance, the receiver must formulate and mail a notification message, sent using a null reverse path in the envelope, addressed to the address in the envelope return path; if that address is null, no notification is sent. To avoid receiving duplicate messages as a result of timeouts, a receiver must seek to minimise the time it takes to respond to the end of data indicator.

Loop detection matters too. Simple counting of the number of Received headers in a message has proved an effective, if rarely optimal, way of detecting loops, and servers using it should use a large rejection threshold, normally at least 100 Received entries. Whatever mechanism is used, servers must be able to detect and stop trivial loops.
sections.plainLanguage:
To find out where to send a message, the server looks up the domain in DNS and follows the mail exchanger records it finds.

There may be several. The client tries them in order of preference, and if one fails it moves to the next.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SMTP mail is inherently insecure, because it is feasible for even fairly casual users to negotiate directly with receiving and relaying servers and create messages that will trick a naive recipient into believing they came from somewhere else. Constructing such a message so that the spoofing cannot be detected by an expert is somewhat harder, but not enough to be a deterrent to someone determined and knowledgeable. Real mail security lies only in end-to-end methods involving the message bodies, such as digital signatures.

Protocol extensions and configuration options that provide authentication at the transport level improve somewhat on this, but unless they are accompanied by careful handoffs of responsibility in a carefully designed trust environment, they remain weaker than end-to-end mechanisms that use digitally signed messages rather than depending on the integrity of the transport. Efforts to make it harder for users to set envelope return path and header From fields to point at addresses other than their own are largely misguided, because they frustrate legitimate applications in which mail is sent by one user on behalf of another or in which replies should go to a special address. This specification advocates only that useful functionality not be disabled in the hope of providing some small margin of protection against an ignorant user trying to fake mail.

Addresses that do not appear in the message headers may appear in RCPT commands, most often because of a mailing address used as a list expander or because of blind copies. Clients and servers should not copy the full set of RCPT arguments into the headers, whether as trace headers or as informational or private-extension headers. Since that rule is often violated in practice and cannot be enforced, sending systems that are aware of blind copy use may find it helpful to send each blind copy as a separate transaction with a single RCPT command. There is no inherent relationship between the envelope addresses and the addresses in the headers, and receiving systems should not try to deduce such relationships and alter the headers accordingly; the popular Apparently-to header violates this principle and is a common source of unintended information disclosure.

Individual sites may want to disable VRFY or EXPN for security reasons. Implementations that permit this must not appear to have verified addresses that are not in fact verified, so a server that disables these commands must return a 252 response rather than a code that could be confused with successful or unsuccessful verification. Returning 250 with the address after checking it only for syntax violates the rule, and so does an implementation that always returns 550 whether or not the address is valid. The contents of mailing lists have become a popular source of addresses for spammers, and the use of EXPN to harvest addresses has increased as list administrators installed protections, so implementations should still support EXPN but sites should carefully evaluate the trade-offs, and some may make EXPN available only to authenticated requestors.

Finally, there is an ongoing debate about the debugging advantages of announcing the server type and version in the greeting or in reply to HELP, against the disadvantage of exposing information useful in a hostile attack. The utility of the debugging information is beyond doubt, and those who argue for making it available point out that it is far better to actually secure an SMTP server than to hope that concealing known vulnerabilities by hiding the server's identity will provide protection.
sections.plainLanguage:
SMTP itself cannot tell you who really sent a message. The addresses in the envelope are whatever the sending machine claims, and anyone can speak to a mail server directly and claim anything.

The only way to be sure a message is genuine is to sign the message itself, end to end, rather than relying on the path it travelled.

messages.label: 250 EXTENSIONS
messages.note: Often a multiline reply listing what the server supports.

messages.label: MESSAGE AND END MARKER
messages.note: The message ends with a line holding only a period.

messages.label: 250 OK
messages.note: The server has taken responsibility for the message.

viz.caption: WHAT THE FIRST DIGIT OF A REPLY CODE MEANS

items.label: POSITIVE PRELIMINARY
items.desc: Accepted, but the action is held pending confirmation in this reply.

items.label: POSITIVE COMPLETION
items.desc: The action succeeded. A new request may begin.

items.label: POSITIVE INTERMEDIATE
items.desc: Accepted, but waiting for further information. Used in DATA.

items.label: TRANSIENT FAILURE
items.desc: Not accepted, but the error is temporary and the action may be retried.

items.label: PERMANENT FAILURE
items.desc: The action will not happen under any circumstances.
